parakeet: Outside religion, the same pattern appears whenever people respond to a messy reality by reaching for a grand abstraction that is even less accountable than the thing they're trying to explain. This is part of why conspiracy thinking is so attractive, why some ideological frameworks become so bloated, and why people reach for giant totalizing stories about the system, the elites, the algorithm, or energy to explain everything. Rather than working through distributed causes, competing incentives, historical contingencies, institutional structures and human contradictions, they adopt an oversized explanation that feels cleaner than reality. The result is that people start preferring explanations not because they're more grounded, but because they're more emotionally satisfying, morally tidy, or narratively complete. The omniscience problem shows up outside religion whenever people act as though persons, systems or futures are more settled and knowable than they really are. Beyond religion, the same impulse appears whenever people overread behavior, overdiagnose identity, or treat open situations like closed cases. This is what happens when someone says people like that always do this, or that person is obviously a narcissist, or that generation is doomed. That algorithm already knows what people want, or we already know how this story ends. It's a secular version of the omniscience fantasy, the desire to turn unfolding reality into something already fixed, legible, and classified. When that becomes common, information no longer serves inquiry very well. It becomes a tool for premature closure. People stop investigating and start pronouncing. They stop learning and start sorting.
